How do I save money?

  • Get Amazon Prime and utilize Prime Pantry. While this sounds like spending money to not save money, it does save time. Time I use for doing other side jobs when not doing my main job. Like fixing peoples' computers. Plus, as a bundle, Prime is very much worthwhile in free shipping alone imo, and it comes with so much other stuff. Travel time is usually the largest time-cost when doing something like buying groceries or whatever.

  • If you can stomach it and aren't allergic to Soy products, use Soylent to replace some meals. You can use it for all meals, but I wouldn't ever recommend that. Again, sounds like it's spending money to not save money, but at 3 meals a day for a week, it comes out to $2.57 per meal. It also saves more time because minimal effort to produce and is "healthy" compared to what other meals you could get for $2.57. But yeah, mix it with regular meals. It's much more manageable then. Also, add a shot of vanilla creamer for coffee to it and it tastes just like an ice cream milk shake.

  • Buy my tires off of Amazon. Combined with the above Prime, this is even better. I have a very hard time finding prices that beat Amazon for tires in my local area. I'd be paying like $20-$30 more if not for that. Reviews say the tires are of high quality and of the ones I've purchased, I've yet to have issues.

  • Change your own oil. Really, it's not that hard. It's literally "Get oil pan or other old oil disposal container -> put under car oil drain -> open drain -> after draining oil stops, close drain -> pour oil into oil inlet in engine compartment until oil dip stick has oil at appropriate level"

Admittedly some cars make that process more complicated, but most don't. And usually mechanic shops don't make money on oil changes. They tend to use those as opportunities to look for other things to sell you (some of the more dubious shops might even try selling you something when you don't need it).

  • Live with a relative and pay them an agreed upon rent. While obviously mixing business with family is bad, it's just more economical to pay what would end up being a reasonable rent (usually) rather than what some places charge for rent just because it's the local norm.

These are just some pro tips about being financially responsible. Not necessarily saving money so much as storing more of it for the future (same concept though).

  • Check if your employer has matching for a savings plan. What this essentially means is that you open a 401(K) through your employer. You tell your employer to take 6% of your paycheck and put it in said savings account. The employer would then match you up to 4% of your paycheck. So you are using 6% of your paycheck to put 10% in the savings account (the extra 4% comes from your employer).

This is pre-tax money. The 4% from your employer is effectively free money. You just don't get to spend it until you retire or withdraw/rollover the 401(K) (which you'd then have to pay taxes on the money so that's not advised).

  • Check if your employer has a Health Savings Account option. An HSA is a savings account for your healthcare costs. It too is pre-tax money and is incentivised by the federal government in similar ways like 401(K)s.

  • Invest the same amount per paycheck into an Index Fund each paycheck you get. This is called Dollar Cost Averaging. The idea is that, yes, the market will have fluctuations, but since you are investing every 2 weeks (or whenever you get paid), the losses on one paycheck's investment are lessened by the gains on another, later, paycheck's investment. It's using the law of big numbers (that they average out in the end) to basically smooth out any ups/downs the market has, so you are more likely to get the average market percentage rate. For the S&P 500, that's around 20% (exceptionally high currently, that's not normal at all). You would want to get an investing account that doesn't charge you for each investment though. Otherwise that'd seriously eat away at whatever gains you get.
